Slides: [Java network concurrency](../slides/09-network-concurrency.qmd)

## Objectives

The TCP servers of [chapter 08](08-tcp-and-udp.qmd) handle one client at a time.
This is not very useful in a production environment.

In this chapter, you get a quick introduction to concurrency, then you learn how
to implement and manage it in Java network applications, to handle several clients
at the same time.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Define what concurrency is, and how it differs from parallelism.
- Define the different ways to handle multiple clients at the same time:
  - Multiprocessing.
  - Multithreading.
  - Asynchronous programming.
- Implement and manage concurrency in Java network applications.
- Choose between platform threads, thread pools and virtual threads.

## Scope

This chapter covers the concurrency a network application needs: handling several
clients at the same time, and sharing data between them safely.

Java has many classes to handle concurrency, in packages such as
`java.util.concurrent`, `java.util.concurrent.atomic` and
`java.util.concurrent.locks`. This chapter uses a few of them, the bare minimum
for this course, without going into the details of each class. Other teaching
units go deeper into concurrency.

What matters most is to understand the concept of concurrency, and how to handle
several clients at the same time in a Java network application.

## Explore the code examples

Alone, in pairs or in groups, **take 10 minutes to explore and discuss the code
examples** in the
[code examples repository]({{< var examples-url >}}/tree/main/09-network-concurrency),
directory `09-network-concurrency`. Pull the latest changes first.

Try to answer the following questions:

- How do the code examples work?
- What are the main takeaways of the code examples?
- What are the main differences between the code examples?

You can use the following content to help you.

## Concurrency: an introduction

In **concurrent** programming, the execution of several tasks overlaps in time: a
task can start without waiting for the others to finish. A long task may take
longer to finish, as it shares the processor with the others. For example, a program updates its window while it downloads data, and a server
accepts a new client while it serves the others.

**Parallelism** is the execution of several tasks at the same instant, on different
cores. It is one way to run concurrent tasks: on a single core, concurrent tasks
take turns; on several cores, they can also run in parallel. Concurrent does not always
mean parallel.

Before diving into concurrency, let's take a step back and remember what a
processor is.

### What is a processor?

A processor is a piece of hardware that executes instructions, very quickly
(billions of instructions per second). It is also called a CPU, for Central
Processing Unit.

Most computers have one processor; some have several. A processor can have one or
more cores: it is then called a multi-core processor.

### What is a core?

A core is a physical unit inside a processor that executes instructions.

For the sake of simplicity, consider that a core executes one instruction, of one
thread, at a time. (Modern cores execute several instructions at once, with
techniques such as pipelining and superscalar execution, and some run two threads
at once.)

With several processors and/or several cores, the machine executes several
instructions at the same time, one per core.

### What is a process?

A process is a program in execution. It is identified by a process ID.

Each process has its own memory space: by default, the other processes do not see
it.

A process is resource-heavy: it is expensive to create and to destroy, compared to
a thread.

Processes communicate with each other through the operating system, with
inter-process communication (IPC): a TCP socket on `localhost`, as in
[chapter 08](08-tcp-and-udp.qmd), a pipe, a file, or a memory area they agree to
share. It is more work than for threads, which share their memory from the start.

### What is a thread?

A thread is a sequence of instructions that runs inside a process, independently of
the other threads of the process. Each thread has its own stack and its own program
counter.

The main thread is the thread created when the application starts. It can then
create other threads to handle other tasks.

The operating system decides which thread runs on which core, and for how long.
This is called
[scheduling](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing)>). On a single
core, it switches between the threads very quickly: they *appear* to run at the
same time. On several cores, several threads can really run at the same time, one per
core: in parallel.

A thread is quite similar to a process, except that it shares the memory of the
other threads of its process. It is therefore much cheaper to create and destroy
than a process (but still more expensive than a simple object). Threads
communicate with each other through this shared memory.

Threads are more lightweight than processes, but the number of threads of the
operating system is limited.

Using threads, a server can manage multiple clients at the same time: each client
is handled by its own thread. On a single core, the clients take turns; on several
cores, several clients can also be served in parallel.

Splitting one computation over several cores, to get its result sooner, is called
[parallel computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_computing). It is quite
complex to implement, and it is not covered in this course.

### What problems can concurrency cause?

Managing multiple clients at the same time is a common requirement for network
applications, and it raises a few questions:

- What happens when a client connects to the server?
- How do you isolate the data sent by one client from the others?
- What happens when multiple clients want to access the same resource (variables)
  at the same time?

### What happens when multiple threads access the same resource?

When multiple threads access the same resource (a variable) at the same time,
problems can occur:

- A thread can read a variable while another thread is writing to it.
- Two threads can write to the same variable at the same time.

The operating system can switch from one thread to another at any time, even in the
middle of a Java statement, and on several cores, two threads run at the same
instant. `count++`, for example, is three steps: read `count`, add one, write
`count`. If two threads read the same value before either of them writes, one of
the increments is lost.

These problems are called **race conditions**. They are the most common problems
when multiple threads access the same resource, and they lead to unexpected
results, errors and crashes. The result depends on the order in which the threads
run, which changes from one execution to the next.

The next sections show how to avoid them.

## Handling one client at a time

A server that handles one client at a time is called an **iterative server**: it
serves the clients one after the other, each one until it leaves. The name says how
the server serves its clients, whatever its number of threads:
`TcpServerSingleThreadExample` has two threads (the main thread and one worker),
and it is still an iterative server.

An iterative server is quite simple to implement:

1. It creates a socket to listen for incoming connections.
2. When a connection is accepted, it gets a socket to communicate with the client.
3. It reads the data sent by the client and sends a response.

Its main drawback: it can only handle one client at a time. Another client that
connects waits until the first one is disconnected (see the note on socket
connection behavior in [chapter 08](08-tcp-and-udp.qmd#tcp-in-the-socket-api)).

In [chapter 08](08-tcp-and-udp.qmd), a TCP connection is like a phone call. A
server is then like a hotline, and an iterative server is a hotline with a single
operator. While the operator talks to a caller, the next callers hear "please hold"
until the call ends. The operating system plays the same role: it accepts the
connections and keeps them waiting until the server calls `accept()`.

An iterative server is suitable for testing and learning purposes. To manage
multiple clients, a server must handle multiple sockets at the same time: a
**concurrent server**.

## Handling multiple clients with concurrency

There are several ways to handle multiple clients concurrently, including:

- Multiprocessing.
- Multithreading.
- Asynchronous programming.

Java has a package for concurrency called
[`java.util.concurrent`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html).

This course focuses on multithreading. The other methods are equally valid and
interesting to learn.

### Multiprocessing

The main process of the application creates other processes, one per client, for
example by copying itself (a *fork*).

A process is heavier than a thread: it is more expensive to create and to destroy,
and the processes communicate with IPC. In exchange, the processes are isolated:
when the process of one client crashes, the others go on. Web servers such as
Apache can work this way.

An analogy is a separate call centre for each caller, with its own building and phone
system.

### Multithreading

The main thread of the application creates other threads to handle the clients,
one thread per client.

Threads are much cheaper than processes, and share the memory of the process. The
number of operating-system threads is still limited.

There are two ways to manage the threads:

1. Unlimited threads: one new thread for each new client.
2. A **fixed thread pool**: a fixed number of threads, reused from one client to
   the next.

With unlimited threads, the analogy is a hotline that hires a new operator for each
call, and adds a desk for them. The more calls arrive, the more operators and desks
are added, until there is no room left in the building (the resources of the
operating system). When the building is full, the next call cannot be answered at
all: the server fails to create the thread (`OutOfMemoryError`). With operating-system threads, this approach is dangerous in
production, as the resources of a system are limited. Virtual threads, presented
below, make it possible.

With a fixed thread pool, the analogy is a hotline with a fixed number of
operators. A new call goes to a free operator; when all of them are busy, the caller
waits on hold until one is free. The
number of threads stays under control, whatever the number of clients. The price:
when all the threads are busy, even with slow clients, the next clients wait.

### Asynchronous programming

Asynchronous programming handles many tasks with a few threads, often a single one.
Instead of blocking until a task completes, the thread starts it and moves on to
other tasks.

It is based on the concept of callbacks: a callback is a function called when a
task is completed.

An analogy is a hotline that says "leave your number, we will call you back". The
caller hangs up and does other things; the hotline calls back when the answer is
ready. A few operators can handle many callers this way.

Asynchronous programming is quite complex to implement, and it is not covered in
this course. You might discover it in other teaching units.
[Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) is a good example of asynchronous programming.

## Handling multiple threads in Java

### Tasks

The work to do for one client goes into a **task**: an object that implements
[`Runnable`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Runnable.html)
(a `run()` method) or
[`Callable`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Callable.html)
(a `call()` method that returns a value). In the code examples, the task is
`ClientHandler`:

```java
static class ClientHandler implements Runnable {
  private final Socket socket;

  public ClientHandler(Socket socket) {
    this.socket = socket;
  }

  @Override
  public void run() {
    // Read from and write to the socket of the client, then close it
  }
}
```

`run()` takes no parameters: the constructor receives what the task needs, here the
socket of the client.

### Running a task on a thread

Calling `run()` or `call()` yourself runs the task on the current thread, like any
method. picocli does exactly this with your commands, which implement `Callable`: it
calls their `call()` method on the main thread.

To run a task on another thread, there are two ways:

- **By hand**: `new Thread(task).start()` creates a thread and starts the task on
  it. `Thread` accepts only a `Runnable`. Server 04 of the code examples does this
  for each client.
- **With an
  [`ExecutorService`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.html)**,
  which manages the threads for you: `submit(task)` runs the task on one of its
  threads. It accepts a `Runnable` or a `Callable`. The
  [`Executors`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html)
  class creates the different implementations of `ExecutorService`, which you
  discover in the code examples. Each one has its own pros and cons.

Servers 03 and 05 to 08 of the code examples follow the same pattern. The main
thread accepts the clients, and submits each new client to the executor, as a
`ClientHandler` task:

```java
try (ServerSocket serverSocket = new ServerSocket(PORT);
    ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) {
  while (!serverSocket.isClosed()) {
    Socket clientSocket = serverSocket.accept();
    executor.submit(new ClientHandler(clientSocket));
  }
}
```

`submit()` returns at once: the main thread goes straight back to `accept()`, while
another thread serves the client. With a fixed pool of 10 threads, up to 10 clients
are served at the same time; the others wait in the queue of the executor.

An `ExecutorService` can also run several methods of one program at the same time. The
`Receiver` of the UDP template of chapter 08, part 2
(`08-tcp-and-udp/templates/java-udp-programming`)
starts two workers, one for the emitters and one for the operators, with a fixed
thread pool of two threads:

```java
@Override
public Integer call() {
  try (ExecutorService executorService = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); ) {
    executorService.submit(() -> runAndReport(this::emittersWorker));
    executorService.submit(() -> runAndReport(this::operatorsWorker));
  } catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("[Receiver] Exception: " + e);

    return 1;
  }

  return 0;
}
```

Each worker reads its own socket in a loop, on its own thread: the receiver listens
to the emitters and to the operators at the same time. At the end of the `try`,
`close()` waits until all the submitted tasks have completed.

`submit()` keeps the exception thrown by a task, without printing it. `runAndReport`
runs the worker and prints its exception, so that you see it.

## Platform threads and virtual threads

Java has two kinds of
[`Thread`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html):

- A **platform thread** is backed by one operating-system thread, for its whole
  life. These are the threads of `new Thread(...)` and of the thread pools.
- A **virtual thread** is managed by the Java virtual machine (JVM), which runs many
  virtual threads on a few platform threads, called carrier threads.
  `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` starts one, and `isVirtual()` tells the two
  kinds apart.

With platform threads, each Java thread holds its own operating-system thread,
whether it works or waits:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph JVM["Java virtual machine"]
        P1[Platform thread 1]
        P2[Platform thread 2]
        P3[Platform thread 3]
    end
    subgraph OS["Operating system"]
        T1[Thread]
        T2[Thread]
        T3[Thread]
    end
    P1 --> T1
    P2 --> T2
    P3 --> T3
    style JVM fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
    style OS fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
```

With virtual threads, many Java threads share a few carrier threads:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph JVM["Java virtual machine"]
        V1[VT 1] & V2[VT 2] & V3[VT 3] --> C1[Carrier thread 1]
        V4[VT 4] & V5[VT 5] & V6[VT 6] --> C2[Carrier thread 2]
    end
    subgraph OS["Operating system"]
        T1[Thread]
        T2[Thread]
    end
    C1 --> T1
    C2 --> T2
    style JVM fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
    style OS fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
```

When a virtual thread blocks on the network (a `readLine()` or an `accept()` on a
socket, for example) or in `Thread.sleep()`, it **unmounts** from its carrier
thread: the JVM runs another virtual thread on the carrier in the meantime. When the
data arrives, the JVM **mounts** the virtual thread again, on a free carrier thread,
and it resumes.

In the hotline analogy, a carrier thread is an operator at a desk, and a virtual
thread is a call. When a call needs an answer from a database, the operator puts it
on hold and takes another call in the meantime. A few desks are enough for many
calls. The JVM decides which
virtual thread runs on which carrier thread; the operating system decides which
carrier thread runs on which core.

A virtual thread is fast to create and takes little memory: a server can create
thousands, even millions of them, one per client. Virtual threads are not faster
than platform threads, only lighter. They help when the tasks spend their time
waiting on the network (clients, databases), as the clients of a server do. For
pure computation, they do no better than a fixed pool of one thread per core: the
number of cores limits the work done at the same time. Virtual threads are
available since Java 21 ([JEP 444](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444)).

`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` starts a new virtual thread for each
task. With it, one thread per client is a good choice for a network server, even
with many clients.

## Thread-safe variable types and data structures in Java

Ordinary variables and collections, such as `int`, `HashMap` or `ArrayList`, give
wrong results when several threads change them at the same time: this is the race
condition of `count++` seen above. With 8 threads that each run `count++` 100,000
times, `count` ends far below 800,000 (between 260,000 and 400,000 in three runs on
a 14-core laptop). A `HashMap` shared by the same 8 threads loses entries in the
same way.

There are two solutions:

- **Locks**: they let only one thread at a time run a piece of code, the
  equivalent of mutexes and semaphores in C/C++. Locks are not covered (and not
  expected to be used) in this course.
- **Thread-safe** variable types and data structures: classes of Java whose methods
  are atomic, so that several threads can call them at the same time.

Java provides thread-safe variable types in the
[`java.util.concurrent.atomic`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/atomic/package-summary.html)
package. Some useful ones:

- `AtomicBoolean`, instead of `boolean`/`Boolean`.
- `AtomicInteger`, instead of `int`/`Integer`.
- `AtomicLong`, instead of `long`/`Long`.

Their methods are **atomic**: `incrementAndGet()` reads, adds one and writes in one
operation, which no other thread can interrupt.

Java provides concurrent collections (data structures) in the
[`java.util.concurrent`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html)
package. Some useful ones:

- `ConcurrentHashMap`, instead of `HashMap`.
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, instead of `ArrayList`, when reads are much more frequent
  than writes: each write copies the whole list.
- `CopyOnWriteArraySet`, instead of `HashSet`, for small sets, with the same
  trade-off.
- `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`, instead of `LinkedList`.

Use them instead of the standard types and collections whenever multiple threads
access the same variable.

Most single calls, such as `get()` or `put()`, are atomic, but two calls in a row
are two operations: another thread can run between them.

A common case is a name that each client must take for itself, as with `JOIN` in
the SMS protocol of [chapter 06](06-application-protocols.qmd). With
`containsKey()` then `put()`, two clients can check the same name at the same
instant, both find it free, and both take it. `putIfAbsent()` checks and takes the
name in one atomic operation: it returns `null` if the name was free and is now
taken, or the current value if another client already has it.

```java
ConcurrentMap<String, Socket> clients = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

if (clients.putIfAbsent(name, socket) == null) {
  // The name is now taken by this client
} else {
  // Another client already has this name
}
```

When several values must be updated together (for example, an `AtomicInteger` and
a `ConcurrentHashMap` at the same time), you need locks again. If you are
interested, see the
[`java.util.concurrent.locks`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/locks/package-summary.html)
package.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Execute the code examples {#sec-ex1}

Return to the code examples and take some time to execute them, understand them and
see the results. Each program is a single Java file, and all the servers listen on
port 1234: run one server at a time, from its directory, in its own terminal:

```sh
java <ExampleName>.java
```

Then, from `01-tcp-client-example`, start three clients at the same time, and watch
when each one gets its answer:

```sh
for i in 1 2 3; do java TcpClientExample.java & done; wait
```

### Exercise 2: Answer the following questions {#sec-ex2}

Using the
[official Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html),
can you answer these questions?

1. Explain the differences between the following implementations:
   - `TcpServerSimpleExample`.
   - `TcpServerSingleThreadExample`.
   - `TcpServerMultiThreadExample`.
   - `TcpServerCachedThreadPoolExample`.
   - `TcpServerFixedThreadPoolExample`.
   - `TcpServerVirtualThreadExample`.
2. What is the difference between a platform thread and a virtual thread?
3. When and why should you use one or the other?
4. Can you explain why `TcpServerSingleThreadExample` does not work as expected?
5. Check the `TcpServerConcurrentDataStructuresExample` code example. Can you explain
   why `AtomicInteger` and `ConcurrentHashMap` are used instead of a standard
   `Integer` and `HashMap`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**1. The implementations.** With three clients started at the same time, and a
server that takes 10 seconds per client:

| Server | Threads | The three clients get their answer after |
|---|---|---|
| `TcpServerSimpleExample` | The main thread only | 10, 20, 30 seconds |
| `TcpServerSingleThreadExample` | One worker thread | 10, 20, 30 seconds |
| `TcpServerMultiThreadExample` | One new thread per client | 10 seconds each |
| `TcpServerCachedThreadPoolExample` | As many as needed, reused | 10 seconds each |
| `TcpServerFixedThreadPoolExample` | A fixed number (2) | 10, 10, 20 seconds |
| `TcpServerVirtualThreadExample` | One virtual thread per client | 10 seconds each |

- `TcpServerSimpleExample` is an iterative server: it handles the client in the main
  thread, which calls `accept()` again only when the client is done. A good starting
  point to understand how TCP works.
- `TcpServerSingleThreadExample` is still an iterative server, but it uses
  [`newSingleThreadExecutor()`](<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newSingleThreadExecutor()>):
  an `ExecutorService` with a single worker thread operating off an unbounded queue.
  The main thread accepts the clients and puts them in the queue; the worker serves
  them one after the other. Changing one line turns it into a server that handles
  several clients, as in the next examples.
- `TcpServerMultiThreadExample` creates a new
  [`Thread`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html)
  for each client, with no limit. Threads are not cheap: each one takes memory, and
  many clients at once can exhaust the resources of the server.
- `TcpServerCachedThreadPoolExample` uses
  [`newCachedThreadPool()`](<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newCachedThreadPool()>):
  it creates new threads as needed, but reuses the threads that are free. A thread
  unused for sixty seconds is terminated. It saves creating threads when clients
  come and go, but it still has no limit: a thousand clients at once take a thousand
  threads.
- `TcpServerFixedThreadPoolExample` uses
  [`newFixedThreadPool(int)`](<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newFixedThreadPool(int)>):
  a fixed number of threads operating off a shared unbounded queue. The third client
  waits in the queue until one of the two threads is free. The number of threads
  stays under control. The difficulty is choosing it: too few threads make the
  clients wait, too many consume too many resources.
- `TcpServerVirtualThreadExample` uses
  [`newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`](<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()>):
  it starts a new virtual thread for each client. Virtual threads are very
  lightweight, so the server can create one per client, even for many clients.

**2. Platform thread and virtual thread.** Both are `Thread` objects. A platform
thread is backed by one operating-system thread. A
[virtual thread](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/core/virtual-threads.html)
is managed by the Java virtual machine (JVM), which runs many virtual threads on a
few platform threads. When a virtual thread blocks, on a `readLine()` or a
`Thread.sleep()` for example, the JVM runs another virtual thread on the platform
thread in the meantime. Virtual threads are available since Java 21.

**3. Which one to use.** It depends on the context and the use case.

- `TcpServerSimpleExample` and `TcpServerSingleThreadExample` are useful for
  understanding how TCP works, not for real-world applications.
- `TcpServerMultiThreadExample` and `TcpServerCachedThreadPoolExample` work for a
  small number of clients, with no protection against too many.
- `TcpServerFixedThreadPoolExample` keeps strict control over the threads. It is
  the choice when each task uses the processor (computations), with about one thread
  per core.
- `TcpServerVirtualThreadExample` is the choice when the clients spend most of their
  time waiting on the network, as the clients of a server usually do.

A rule of thumb: with Java 21 or later, as in this course, use virtual threads for a
network server.

**4. The single-thread example.** It reads and writes with
`StandardCharsets.US_ASCII`, but the messages contain an emoji (👋), which is not an
ASCII character. The server decodes the four UTF-8 bytes of the emoji as four
invalid characters (`����`), and encodes its own emoji as `?`. If you use the wrong
encoding, the message cannot be decoded correctly: both sides must use the same one
([chapter 04](04-java-io.qmd)).

**5. The concurrent data structures.** All the client threads use the same counter
and the same map. With an `int`, `totalNumberOfClients++` from two threads at the
same time can lose an increment; `incrementAndGet()` is atomic. Two threads writing
to a `HashMap` at the same time can corrupt it; a `ConcurrentHashMap` stays
consistent.

Start three clients at the same time: the server prints `last time this client
connected: null` three times. The three threads call `get()` before any of them
calls `put()`: each call is atomic, the pair is not. `put()` returns the previous value, in one
atomic operation:

```java
Date lastConnection = clientConnections.put(clientHostname, new Date());
```
:::

### Exercise 3: Many connections at once {#sec-ex3}

Write a client and a server that use virtual threads:

- The server sends back every line it receives (an echo server).
- The client opens many connections (for example 100), as fast as possible. On each
  connection, it sends 1,000 messages in a loop, and reads the answer to each one.

Then evaluate the performance of the server:

1. Measure the time taken by the 100 connections with virtual threads, inside the
   client with `System.nanoTime()`.
2. Replace the virtual threads with a single-thread executor, in the client and in
   the server. Measure again.
3. From the two measures, compute how much faster the work goes with virtual
   threads.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`solutions/echo-many-connections` in the code examples takes the kind of thread as
an argument: `java EchoServer.java single` and `java EchoClient.java single` use a
single thread; without the argument, they use virtual threads.

On a laptop with 14 cores, the client prints about 1.9 seconds with a single
thread, and 0.8 seconds with virtual threads: the work goes about 2.4 times faster.

With a single thread, the connections are served one after the other. With virtual
threads, the 100 connections are open and served at the same time: that is
concurrency. But the work goes only about 2.4 times faster, far from 14 times: the
client and the server run on the same machine and share its cores, and each wait
for the next line is very short, so there is little waiting to overlap.
Concurrency gains the most when the tasks wait longer, as the benchmark in
[*Go further*](#go-further) shows.

Measured with `time java EchoClient.java`, the same runs take about 2.2 and
1.45 seconds: `time` also counts the start of Java and the compilation of the file,
about 0.6 seconds.
:::

### Benchmark the servers

The directory `benchmark` of the code examples holds a server that takes its
strategy as an argument, and a client that opens 1,000 connections at the same
time and sends one request on each. A request is `SLEEP` (the server waits 100 ms,
like a slow database) or `COMPUTE` (the server computes for about 6 ms). The client
prints the number of requests per second:

```sh
# In one terminal: single, thread, cached, fixed-<n> or virtual
java BenchmarkServer.java virtual

# In another one
java BenchmarkClient.java SLEEP
```

Requests per second, measured on Linux with Java 25 and 14 cores, with the client on
the same machine:

| Server | `SLEEP` | `COMPUTE` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `single` (iterative) | 10 | 170 to 175 |
| `thread` (one platform thread per client) | 2,300 to 2,800 | 1,200 to 1,300 |
| `cached` | 2,800 to 3,000 | 1,400 |
| `fixed-4` | 39 | 655 to 673 |
| `fixed-14` (one thread per core) | 134 | 1,310 to 1,530 |
| `fixed-500` | 2,400 to 2,600 | 1,360 |
| `virtual` | 4,500 to 5,800 | 1,330 to 1,500 |

- With `SLEEP`, the tasks wait. Every 100 ms, a fixed pool handles at most as many
  requests as it has threads: 40 requests per second with 4 threads, 140 with 14. Virtual threads
  handle the most requests.
- With `COMPUTE`, the cores limit the work. 14 threads, one per core, do as well as
  1,000; 4 threads use only 4 cores. Virtual threads are not faster than platform
  threads.

The numbers depend on the machine: measure yours.

### Concurrency and parallelism

The video [Concurrency Vs Parallelism!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RlM9AfWf1WU)
by ByteByteGo explains the difference between the two, with examples.

## Conclusion

In this chapter, you have learned how to handle multiple clients at the same time
using concurrency.

With chapter 08, you have all the knowledge to create your own TCP and UDP network
applications in a robust and efficient way: a chat server, a file server, a web
server, games, etc.
